source: Eielts, Pouw, Ouwehand, van Gog, Zwaan, Paas (2020) Co-thought gesturing supports more complex problem solving in subjects with lower visual working-memory capacity (Psychological Research 84:502-513)
finding: Resolves the 72 vs 73 count. Total analysed sample is 73. Group membership was defined per task, so groups differ by task. 3-disc: non-gesturing 27, spontaneous 11, instructed 35 (=73). 4-disc: 19, 18, 35 (=72). The 4-disc regression table itself reports N=72. So there is no unexplained participant. Also: the author list in earlier files (a16, a17) was wrong. First author is Eielts, not Pouw.
numbers: 76 recruited; 1 technical exclusion; 2 excluded for not following the gesture instruction; 73 analysed. 4-disc solution-time model explained 37% of variance. VPT x spontaneous gesturing t(68)=2.88, p=.005; VPT x instructed gesturing t(68)=2.42, p=.018. No main effects of gesture group. VPT main effect t(68)=-5.44, p<.001.
limits: Per-task group assignment means the spontaneous group is self-selected and larger on the hard task (11 to 18). One 4-disc participant is missing from the table (N=72), consistent with the paper.
agent_relevance: Correct the source label for K06 (Eielts et al. 2020). The benefit appears only as an interaction with capacity, never as a main effect.

source: Eielts et al. (2020) Johnson-Neyman regions and Corsi control
finding: Per-capacity result for the 4-disc task. Instructed gesturing helped only people with low visual working memory (VPT), roughly the bottom quarter. Spontaneous gesturing helped the bottom third. The highest-VPT people were slightly slowed by gesturing. Spatial working memory (Corsi) showed no interaction.
numbers: Instructed gesturing: significant benefit for centred VPT below -0.13 (26.4% of sample), t(52) -2.63 to -2.01, p .011 to .050; slowed above 0.36 (1.89% of sample). Spontaneous: benefit below -0.083 (33.3%), t(32) -2.93 to -2.04, p .050 to .006; slowed above 0.26 (2.8%). Corsi interactions on 4-disc: not significant (spontaneous p=.803, instructed p=.927).
limits: Regions of significance are edge-sensitive with small cells. Only about a quarter of the sample sits in the benefit zone. Solution time, not steps or accuracy.
agent_relevance: Supports a cost rule: externalise when internal capacity is low and difficulty is high. A tiny high-capacity tail may be slowed, so do not force it for strong cases.

source: Goldin-Meadow, Nusbaum, Kelly, Wagner (2001) Explaining math: gesturing lightens the load. Psychological Science 12(6):516-522
finding: Founding dual-task study. People explained a maths problem and also held a word or letter list in memory. They remembered more when they gestured than when they did not. Effect held for children and adults. Group means are in figures only, so raw means could not be extracted.
numbers: Analysed 26 children (mean age 9y11m) and 32 adults. Recall when gesturing vs not: children F(1,24)=11.32, p=.003; adults F(1,31)=4.47, p=.04. Long (taxing) lists: children F(1,24)=15.40, p<.001; adults F(1,31)=5.03, p=.03. Short lists: children F(1,24)=3.17 n.s.; adults F(1,31)=0.43 n.s. No interaction with math knowledge F(1,24)=0.63 n.s.
limits: Within-subject; the instruction to keep hands still is itself a task. Analysis only on people who gestured when allowed. Small samples. Verbal load only. Group means are not in the text.
agent_relevance: Effect is load-dependent: only the taxing list showed it. Matches the idea that an external channel matters when working memory is full.

source: Goldin-Meadow et al. (2001) control analyses
finding: Three rival explanations were checked. Explaining longer did not help (explanation time was slightly longer when gesturing, which would predict worse recall, yet recall was better). Being told to hold still did not add load (recall no different when people chose not to gesture versus were told not to). Solving the math correctly did not explain it.
numbers: Explanation time gesturing vs not: children 12.9 s (SD 7.0) vs 11.1 s (SD 5.5); adults 27.7 s (SD 16.7) vs 26.6 s (SD 13.9). Chose vs instructed no gesture: children F(1,8)=0.001, adults F(1,9)=0.003, both n.s. Long-list gain when gesturing vs not by choice or by instruction: children F(1,8)=5.71 p=.04 and 14.11 p=.006; adults F(1,9)=8.07 p=.02 and 7.37 p=.02. These use only 9 children and 10 adults who gestured on some trials.
limits: The inhibition control rests on 9 children and 10 adults. Not preregistered. No same-design repeat found in this pass.
agent_relevance: Answers the effort-of-inhibition worry only partly. It shows the original design addressed this confound.

source: Chu and Kita (2011) The nature of gestures' beneficial role in spatial problem solving. J Exp Psych: General 140:102-116. Experiment 1
finding: Experiment 1 (accepted manuscript). Shepard-Metzler mental rotation, 24 trials. People gestured more on harder trials (bigger rotation angles). Gesturing was spontaneous only, so no causal test here.
numbers: N=132 students. Mean 19.91 of 24 correct (SD 3.51). Mean RT 11.36 s (SD 6.58). 792 gestures, 745 (94.07%) representational. Representational gestures on 2.43 of 24 trials (SD 4.26). Main effect of angle on errors: F(3,393)=87.40, partial eta2=.40.
limits: Correlational. Preprint copy, not copy of record.
agent_relevance: Externalising rises with difficulty, which fits a cost-triggered tool rather than an always-on habit.

source: Chu and Kita (2011) Experiment 2
finding: Three groups: gesture-encouraged, gesture-allowed, gesture-prohibited (sat on hands). Encouraged group beat both others in block 1 and in a second block where gesture was banned for all. KEY: the allowed and prohibited groups did NOT differ. So the data support a boost from encouragement, not an impairment from prevention. No benefit on digit span, so the effect is not general.
numbers: N=66 (22 per group). Group main effect on errors F(2,63)=4.51, partial eta2=.13; block F(1,63)=89.08, eta2=.59; interaction n.s. F(2,63)=0.43. Fisher LSD: encouraged better than prohibited p<.01 and allowed p<.05 in both blocks. Gesture trials in block 1: encouraged 8.86 of 24 (SD 8.55) vs allowed 1.64 (SD 3.63). Gesture rate per minute 3.93 (SD 4.64) vs 0.62 (SD 1.47), t(42)=3.19, d=0.96. Digit span errors: F(2,62)=0.52, p=.60 (.56, .60, .62).
limits: Per-group n is 22. Fisher LSD post hoc is lenient. Encouraged is not the same as spontaneous. Group means for mental rotation are in a figure.
agent_relevance: Changes K05: no evidence here that removing a tool harms performance. Only a forced-use group gained. Test scaffold forcing, not only scaffold removal.

source: Chu and Kita (2011) Experiment 3 (paper folding) and internalisation
finding: Benefit transferred to a different spatial task (paper folding) that needs similar transformations. Gesture frequency fell as people solved more problems, which the authors read as the computation becoming internal. In the encouraged group, trials with gesture were solved a little better than those without (marginal).
numbers: N=32 (encouraged vs allowed). Paper folding errors lower in encouraged group t(30)=2.57, p<.05, d=0.91. Gestures per 24 trials 7.63 (SD 6.11) for encouraged; rate 2.68 (SD 2.75) vs 0.26 (SD 0.72), t(30)=3.41, d=1.20. Gesture frequency fell across sections t(30)=2.03, p=.05, d=0.69. Gesturing trials better than non-gesturing: .56 vs .44, t(28)=1.86, p=.07, d=0.57.
limits: Two groups of 16. The key within-person comparison is marginal (p=.07). Internalisation is an interpretation.
agent_relevance: Supports fading with expertise: externalise early, then internalise. An agent cannot internalise at inference, so this analogy stops at fine-tuning.

source: Alibali, Spencer, Knox, Kita (2011) Spontaneous gestures influence strategy choices in problem solving. Psychological Science 22(9):1138-1144. Experiment 1
finding: Gear-prediction problems. Gesture allowed (feet restrained) vs prohibited (hands in Velcro gloves on a board). Prevention changed WHICH strategy people used, not whether they were right. Prohibited people moved to the abstract parity rule more.
numbers: 88 recruited, 3 excluded (N=85). Accuracy equal: .91 (SD .14) allowed vs .91 (SD .12) prohibited. Parity strategy on at least one trial: .74 allowed vs .91 prohibited, chi2(1, N=85)=4.17, p=.04. Per trial, parity used on 30% of trials with gesture, 76% with no gesture by choice, 52% prohibited by design.
limits: Strategy effect is moderate. The between-trial comparison is correlational. Feet restraint in the control.
agent_relevance: Externalising steers strategy toward simulation. It does not by itself raise accuracy. Do not claim accuracy gains from gesture-like tools without a check.

source: Alibali et al. (2011) Experiment 2 (silent solving)
finding: Within the same paper, a repeat without talking aloud (UK sample). Same strategy effect, again no accuracy difference. Of 52 allowed participants, 28 gestured. Spontaneous non-gesturers used parity more than gesturers.
numbers: Accuracy gesture allowed M=89% (SD 18) vs prohibited M=86% (SD 16), Wald Z=0.91, p=.36. Prohibited vs allowed gesturers: chi2(1,N=85)=3.85, p<.05. Allowed non-gesturers vs gesturers: chi2(1,N=52)=6.52, p=.01.
limits: Same lab and design, so one independent source. Not preregistered.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 5 only in part: this is a replication of a strategy effect, not an accuracy effect.

source: Wassenburg, de Koning, van der Schoot (2018) In which direction to move? Facilitative and interference effects of gestures on problem solver's thinking. J Cogn Psychol
finding: Larger, more ecological Tower of Hanoi test of the Beilock and Goldin-Meadow (2010) gesture-then-reversal result. Gesturing during explanation helped later solving, but the interference from incompatible gestures that earlier work reported was not found. Authors say the gesture effect is not as strong as previously suggested.
numbers: Solution time fell from TOH1 M=66.58 s (SD 29.43) to TOH2 M=52.99 s (SD 22.00) across all participants. Learning gain larger after explaining with gestures. Interference effect of reversed disc move direction: not significant. Only abstract, design and first results were read; the full interaction tests were not extracted.
limits: Compatible-gesture work, not gesture prevention. The interference part is the failed replication. Full F values not read.
agent_relevance: A failed replication of the strong harm claim. Externalising helps a bit; wrong externalising does not clearly hurt.

source: Kirk and Lewis (2017) Gesture facilitates children's creative thinking. Psychological Science (accepted manuscript)
finding: Alternative Uses Task with children. Restricting gesture did not significantly reduce fluency (Experiment 1). Encouraging gesture raised fluency a lot (Experiment 2), but not originality or flexibility. So the gain is in quantity of ideas.
numbers: Exp 1: N=78 (47 gesturers, 27 non-gesturers). Fluency gesturers 10.60 (SD 5.44) vs non-gesturers 8.00 (SD 5.91), t(72)=-1.92, p=.059. Within-child (n=30 gesturers by choice): allowed 9.57 (SD 8.57) vs restricted 8.03 (SD 7.34), t(29)=1.17, p=.251. Exp 2: N=54 (27 per group): fluency 37.67 (SD 16.18) vs control 24.52 (SD 10.00), t(43.35)=3.59, p=.001, d=0.98. Originality .86 vs .85, flexibility .90 vs .91, both n.s.
limits: Children aged 8 to 11. Encouragement means explicit instruction to show uses with the hands.
agent_relevance: Externalisation may raise idea count, not idea quality. Prevention again shows no significant drop.

source: Frith and Miller (2024) Creativity in motion: examining the impact of meaningful movement on creative cognition. Frontiers in Cognition 3:1386375
finding: Largest adult test. Three groups did three Alternative Uses Tasks. Changes in fluency, flexibility and originality did not interact with group. Baseline gesture habit mattered: frequent gesturers scored higher originality in the gesture and meaningless-movement groups than restricted ones, infrequent gesturers scored lower in the gesture group.
numbers: N=151: gesture n=51, meaningless movement n=50, restricted n=50. Group-by-trial interactions n.s. for fluency, flexibility, originality. Baseline gesture frequency positively associated with all four creativity outcomes.
limits: Read from the abstract on the article page. Exact coefficients were not extracted. Exploratory moderation.
agent_relevance: Supports the null on mean externalisation effect for creativity (gap 9): the effect depends on the person, so for an agent it would depend on the model and task, not on the tool alone.

source: Rajpal, Premsri, Kordjamshidi (2026) Spatial Reasoning via Modality Switching Between Language and Symbolic Representations (arXiv 2606.31285v3)
finding: Models first write the story as a grid (an external scratch state), then reason on it. On StepGame, accuracy rose for every model. The gain was NOT biggest for the weakest models. Written relation triples without geometry did not help and often hurt, so the benefit is the spatial layout, not just writing something down.
numbers: StepGame overall accuracy, text then pruned grid (n=5,000; GPT-5.1 n=1,250): LLaMA3.1-70B 44.7 -> 86.7 (+42.0); Qwen3-8B 59.2 -> 84.8 (+25.6); Qwen3-14B 67.8 -> 84.2 (+16.4); Qwen3-32B 67.0 -> 84.1 (+17.1); GPT-5.1 74.3 -> 88.1 (+13.8); LLaMA3.1-8B 19.8 -> 33.3 (+13.5). Relational triples: LLaMA-70B 42.1, Qwen3-32B 60.6, GPT-5.1 64.5 (below text for these three). ToT-CoT baseline: Qwen3-8B 51.3, LLaMA-70B 78.8. Relation extraction F1 94.3 to 95.0 on StepGame; grid construction F1 86.7 to 89.7 from extracted relations.
limits: Grids are built by a pipeline with extra calls, so tokens are not matched. Synthetic benchmarks (StepGame, SpaRTUN, ReSQ). Gains on SpaRTUN are smaller (up to 8%) and on ReSQ up to 5%.
agent_relevance: Closest direct LLM analogue of a gesture-as-external-state scaffold. Gain is large, but it is not a clean capacity story (gap 2) and cost is high (gap 1).

source: Rajpal et al. (2026) Table 21 token cost and adaptive switching
finding: The grid route costs many times more tokens than text, so the gains are not at equal budget. Adaptive switching (use the grid only when the text answer is untrusted or the problem is complex) cuts cost relative to always using the grid on one dataset and not on the other. Gain over grid-only is small.
numbers: Average tokens text vs grid pipeline: StepGame Qwen3-32B 2,012 vs 19,218; LLaMA3.1-70B 272 vs 15,472; GPT-5.1 249 vs 15,727. SpaRTUN Qwen3-32B 1,973 vs 28,113; LLaMA-70B 1,122 vs 31,171; GPT-5.1 1,145 vs 26,951. Adaptive switching: SpaRTUN token cost 6.4% to 12.0% below grid-only with accuracy equal or up to +0.9; StepGame token cost from -0.4% to +10.6% with accuracy +0.4 to +1.6 (GPT-5.1 +1.6 at +10.6% tokens). Adaptive accuracy on StepGame: Qwen3-32B 84.4, LLaMA-70B 83.6, GPT-5.1 85.2. Weakest model LLaMA3.1-8B switches 94.0% of the time.
limits: Switching signals need extra model calls. Thresholds tuned on a validation split. No token-matched text baseline (for example text with 10x sampling) is reported.
agent_relevance: First LLM evidence on choosing when to externalise (gap 7). Selection helps a little. Always externalising works at 10 to 60 times the tokens. Test against best-of-N text at the same cost.

source: Huang, Liu, He, Gilpin (2026) Learning to Draw ASCII Improves Spatial Reasoning in Language Models (arXiv 2604.14641)
finding: Models read ASCII grids well but draw them badly (read-write asymmetry). When the model drew its own ASCII sketch before answering, accuracy fell below text-only. Training on construction (drawing from text) improved later text-only spatial reasoning and transferred to other benchmarks. Humans benefited from being given ASCII (86.6% to 98.1%).
numbers: Text-only accuracy across models 42.0% (Qwen2.5-7B) to 93.3% (GPT-OSS-20B). Generated ASCII accuracy only 12 to 50%; GPT-OSS-20B fails to build a correct layout in 56% of cases. Draw-first-then-answer fell below text-only for all base models. Qwen3-30B fine-tuned on construction, zero-shot, no ASCII at inference, change vs base: StepGame (base 54.9) +9.9; bAbI task 19 (base 17.8) +17.0; SpartQA (base 26.5) +43.3. Comprehension-only training: -6.1 on StepGame. Bidirectional: +8.4, +20.6, +49.0. Human study 11 evaluators: 0.866 description-only vs 0.981 with ASCII (+11.5%).
limits: The transfer gains come from fine-tuning, not from a prompt. Synthetic benchmark. Human study has 3 sets of 10 problems.
agent_relevance: Key for gap 6: self-made external state fails when construction is unreliable. Verify the sketch before relying on it.

source: Lei et al. (2026) SVoT: State-aware Visualization-of-Thought for Spatial Reasoning via Reinforcement Learning (arXiv 2606.11770)
finding: Trained interleaved visual and text state tracking. Removing the generated images from the trained model hurts a lot on interaction-heavy tasks, so images carry real state. But the hardest domain stays near floor and visual quality tracks transition-reasoning correctness.
numbers: Ablation, free-response, size 4 (ID/OOD): Sokoban 78.3/68.3 with visualisations vs 35.0/25.0 without; FrozenLake 83.3/68.3 vs 78.3/65.0; Gather 50.0/16.7 vs 23.3/8.3. MVoT baseline on size 4 Sokoban 15.0/3.3. Largest gain over MVoT 65 points (Sokoban size 4). Size 6 Gather: 6.7/1.7 with images, 0.0/0.0 without. 120 test instances per domain-size pair.
limits: Fine-tuned model (Anole, LoRA, GRPO), small test sets (120), not a prompt-only test. Not token-matched.
agent_relevance: Images help when state transitions are hard to track in text, and still fail when the task has multi-object counting load. Fits the failure-feature story in gap 6.

source: Wu et al. (2024) Mind's Eye of LLMs: Visualization-of-Thought Elicits Spatial Reasoning in LLMs (arXiv 2404.03622v3), re-read
finding: Re-read of the failure analysis. CORRECTION to the earlier critique: the 24 to 26% state-accuracy figure is for visual navigation and visual tiling, not for ring navigation. The ring result is a separate, smaller loss for VoT: the task reduces to modular arithmetic, so drawing adds nothing. Weaker models gained unreliably.
numbers: State visualisation: navigation compliance 51.14, accuracy 26.48, understanding when state correct 65.16; tiling 52.01, 24.25, 77.20. Ring navigation (ring size 12, N=200): GPT-4 CoT 52.5% vs VoT 49.5%. Weaker models: GPT-3.5 CoT guesses randomly in nearly half of route-planning cases; LLaMA3-70B VoT significantly beats CoT on all tasks except tiling. Authors' limitation: effect depends on emergent ability and on prompts.
limits: The Table 3 extraction was garbled, so exact small-model numbers are not recorded. Ring result is a single 200-item test.
agent_relevance: A feature predicting failure: the task is solvable by direct symbolic computation, so a sketch is waste. Gap 6 and gap 2 partly closed.

source: Zeller et al. (2026) MentisOculi: Revealing the Limits of Reasoning with Mental Imagery (arXiv 2602.02465v2, ICML 2026)
finding: Stratified multi-step visual puzzles (for example Rush Hour, hinge folding, paper fold). No evidence that self-generated imagery (latent, interleaved, video) beats text-only reasoning. Unified models fail from compounding generation errors and from failing to use even correct oracle images. Frontier text models can solve a lossless text transcription of Rush Hour.
numbers: No gain from Gemini 3 to Gemini 3-I or from Gemini 2.5 to 2.5-I; text-only MLLMs often beat unified models. Oracle visuals lift unified models on Form Board far above chance but in hinge folding and paper fold only close the gap to the base text model. Raising reasoning tokens (GPT-5.1 used about 13x more under high reasoning) left accuracy largely unchanged. Tool use gave no meaningful gains. Latent-visual model Mirage beat MLLMs at levels 2 to 3 after fine-tuning on 200 samples per level but fell to near chance at level 5.
limits: Procedural puzzles chosen to be hard for text. Tests generated imagery, not a typed grid. Exact accuracies are in figures.
agent_relevance: Best counter-evidence: more reasoning tokens and imagery both gave no benefit here, so the equal-token claim in gap 1 stays unproven. Also shows token count alone does not help.

source: Tong et al. (2026) SwimBird: Eliciting Switchable Reasoning Mode in Hybrid Autoregressive MLLMs (arXiv 2602.06040)
finding: A model trained to choose among text-only, vision-only (latent visual thoughts) and interleaved reasoning per query. It picks text for symbolic math and visual modes for perception-heavy tasks. It beat fixed-pattern baselines on both kinds of benchmark.
numbers: Qwen3-VL-8B base. V* Bench 85.5, HR-Bench 4K 79.0, HR-Bench 8K 74.9 vs Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct 83.8/76.5/71.3. WeMath 49.5 vs 38.8, DynaMath 67.2 vs 65.3, MathVerse_MINI 65.8 vs 61.3, MMStar 71.2 vs 64.7, RealWorldQA 73.1 vs 71.8. Mode distribution: DynaMath and MathVerse almost always text; vision-only share rises from HR-Bench 4K to 8K.
limits: Supervised on 92K curated traces (SwimBird-SFT-92K), so the choice is learned, not prompted. Instruct baseline reproduced by the authors. Latent tokens are continuous states, not human-readable sketches.
agent_relevance: Supports gap 7: learned selection of when to externalise works and avoids the cost of always doing it. No token-matched comparison was found in what was read.

source: Dalumura Hettige and Oppenlaender (2026) PainterBench: A Figural Divergent-Thinking Benchmark for Tool-Using Language Models (arXiv 2609.34195)
finding: Agents draw on a canvas by tool calls, observe it each turn and decide when to stop. Agent drawings rated more creative but less recognisable than human drawings. It does NOT compare drawing against not drawing, so it cannot say whether externalising helps creativity.
numbers: 14 models, 2,700 agent drawings, 300 human reference drawings, 72,000 crowd ratings. Creativity 0.56 agents vs 0.41 humans. Recognisability 0.45 vs 0.53 (difference -0.08, 95% CI -0.11 to -0.06, d=-0.41). Median trial 8 rounds and 9 tool calls (mean 14.5 rounds, SD 21.3). Automated scorer ViDrA-adapted r=0.85 on held-out split.
limits: Benchmark, not an ablation. Creativity ratings by crowd workers, not on the same scale as the Alternative Uses Task.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: a generation task with externalisation exists, but evidence of benefit is missing.

source: Liu et al. (2026) Beyond Description: Cognitively Benchmarking Fine-Grained Action for Embodied Agents (CFG-Bench, arXiv 2511.18685v4)
finding: Closest thing found to an embodied-action test for LLMs (gap 8). Multimodal models are far below humans at describing fine-grained physical action. This is action understanding from video, not finger counting or gesture-assisted reasoning, so it does not test the gesture-for-thinking claim.
numbers: 1,368 videos, 19,562 QA pairs. Top model Gemini-3-Pro 65.60% close-ended, 5.67 open-ended score. Human baseline 95.85% close-ended, 9.05 open-ended. Fine-tuning on the data improved other embodied benchmarks.
limits: Video perception. No finger-counting, action-simulation or gesture-assisted arithmetic task was found in two searches and a handful of arXiv queries.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 stays open: no LLM study of gesture-like help for the model's own reasoning was found. Do not cite CFG-Bench as a test.

source: Bian et al. (2026) Optical Reasoning: Rethinking Images as an Expressive Reasoning Medium Beyond Text (arXiv 2606.09585)
finding: Renders reasoning steps as images and lets the model reason from them. Claims matched or better accuracy with fewer reasoning tokens. This is a compression result on language and math tasks, not a spatial externalisation test. Only the abstract and introduction were read.
numbers: Average reasoning-token cut 28.57% on language tasks and 16% on multimodal tasks; 1.96x token efficiency of text under the authors' own Marginal Accuracy Gain metric.
limits: Own efficiency metric. Not spatial. Method and tables not read.
agent_relevance: Only budget-aware result found, but it is about compressing rationale, not an equal-token gain from externalised state. Gap 1 stays open.

source: Zhao et al. (2026) STAR: Mitigating Cascading Errors in Spatial Reasoning via Turn-point Alignment and Segment-level DPO (arXiv 2604.00558)
finding: Says Visualization-of-Thought suffers cascading errors on complex mazes. Trains on turn-point annotations. Evidence on failure features: long horizon and complex topology.
numbers: STAR 32B success rate 29.27% vs DeepSeek-V3 25.00%; reaches 82.4% of GPT-4's success rate. RedMaze-23K dataset.
limits: Abstract, introduction and results only. Fine-tuned model. Absolute success rates are low.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: failure grows with path length because one wrong drawn state propagates.
